S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.

subtypes.Skin Defects: Excessive preoccupation with practically invisible acne, scars, or complexion.
subtypes.Facial Features: Preoccupation with the shape or size of the nose, eyes, or mouth, which appear normal to others.
subtypes.Asymmetry: Excessive obsession with the face or body not being perfectly symmetrical.
subtypes.Muscle Dysmorphia: The belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite being normal or muscular.
subtypes.Specific Body Parts: Obsession that specific parts like hair, teeth, or chest are ugly or abnormal.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.

subtypes.Mirror Checking or Avoidance: Compulsively checking oneself in the mirror frequently or, conversely, avoiding mirrors strictly.
subtypes.Excessive Camouflaging: Spending excessive time and effort to hide perceived flaws using makeup, clothes, hats, or sunglasses.
subtypes.Skin Picking: Picking or manipulating the skin excessively to remove or 'fix' flaws.
subtypes.Reassurance Seeking: Repetitively asking others for confirmation that one's appearance is okay or not strange.
subtypes.Comparing: Constantly comparing one's body parts with those of passersby or celebrities.
subtypes.Seeking Cosmetic Procedures: Repeatedly seeking or receiving plastic surgery or dermatological procedures.

symptom.disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear minor to others, leading to significant distress or impairment. Individuals typically engage in repetitive behaviors or mental acts (e.g., mirror checking, camouflaging, comparing) in response to these concerns. Onset is often in adolescence but the course is usually chronic, with symptoms waxing and waning and frequently remaining secretive for years before formal help is sought. BDD is distinguished from normal appearance concerns and from eating disorders by the intensity of the preoccupation, the time-consuming rituals, and the focus on specific perceived flaws rather than primarily on weight or shape as a whole.

patient.stressor: Lawson’s preoccupation with his appearance began to stand out to his family after he was diagnosed with hypertension and his primary care doctor strongly emphasized diet and lifestyle changes, repeatedly referencing his weight and cardiovascular risk. Around the same time, he started attending more medical appointments and community health screenings, where he felt intensely scrutinized about his aging body, especially his facial skin and midsection, which he had long been privately self-conscious about but could previously ignore amid farm work and art. As he cut back on heavier farm labor due to joint pain and shifted to mentoring and grant writing, he spent more hours indoors, scrutinizing old photos and mirrors in his studio instead of being absorbed in physical work and community events, and he began turning down invitations to play guitar or exhibit his watercolors because he felt too "embarrassed" by how he looked. His wife eventually urged him to seek psychiatric help after he skipped a follow-up cardiology appointment and a long-planned family reunion because he was convinced others would be focused on his perceived physical flaws, despite reassurance from family and his pastor that nothing about his appearance had meaningfully changed.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop thinking about how bad I look, especially my face and stomach, and it’s gotten to where I don’t want people to see me anymore.”

patient.stressor: Shamis’s appearance concerns intensified after she moved from high school into full-time retail work, where she felt constantly on display under bright store lighting and security cameras, and where managers stressed having a “put-together” look for customer service scores. A supervisor’s offhand comment about “looking more polished for the front register” landed heavily on preexisting insecurities she had about specific facial features from her teen years, and she started spending more and more of her limited income and time trying to “fix” what she saw as unacceptable flaws before each shift. Her meticulous, perfectionistic nature that had once been channeled into puzzles and sales tracking became increasingly focused on scrutinizing photos from work events and comparing herself to coworkers and influencers online, leading her to turn down social invitations and call out of shifts when she felt she “looked wrong.” When she began arriving late because she could not leave the house until she felt her appearance was under control, and a threatened write-up jeopardized the promotion she’d been working toward, she accepted her mother’s suggestion to see a mental health professional through the company’s insurance network.
patient.chief_complaint: “I spend so long checking and fixing how I look before work that I’m missing shifts and still feel like my face looks completely wrong.”

patient.stressor: Danny’s concerns about his appearance, especially around visible scars and perceived asymmetry in his jaw from an old sports injury, had been a quiet background worry since his late teens, but they escalated when his school shifted more heavily to online learning and video-based teaching during the pandemic. Seeing his own image reflected back for hours each day on camera, alongside neatly framed colleagues and polished education influencers on social media, made him acutely self-conscious, and he began avoiding turning on his camera in staff meetings and spending long evenings taking and deleting selfies while experimenting with angles and lighting. As in-person teaching resumed, he found himself dreading parent nights, school photos, and even pickup basketball because he was convinced others were noticing and judging his "crooked" features, leading him to cut back on social activities that had previously helped him cope with stress. After a close friend from the cycling club pointed out how out of character it was for him to dodge group photos and live music outings and suggested that his worries about his looks seemed "way out of proportion," Danny agreed to see a psychiatrist recommended by the school’s employee assistance program.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m constantly hung up on how my face looks on camera and in person, and it’s making me avoid people and things I used to enjoy.”
